We introduce `housepi`, a package for the study of epidemiological datasets from household outbreaks.
In this vignette we'll walk through the process of loading a model, associating necessary definitions to perform inference and simulations.

# The Housepi Model Class

The central element of the package is the class `HousepiModel`, an [R6 class](https://r6.r-lib.org/articles/Introduction.html), used to wrap an Rcpp environment.
We show how to generate a new instance of such a class with a template model, the chain binomial:

```{r}
# import the library 'housepi'
library(housepi)
# set general seed
set.seed(42)

# generate an instance of the chain binomial model
hhmodel <- new_housepi_model("chain-binomial")
```

At any moment we can retrieve the template model description by using the method `$help()`.

## An Expanding Library of Template Household Models

To see the complete list of available template models, from within Rstudio just run

```{r}
# present the list of template model name
template_household_model()
```

Each template comes with its template definitions that can be used straight away or changed.
To know more about each model, choose a name from the previous list and run, e.
g.

```{r}
#| eval: false
# show model description in RStudio help window
template_household_model("chain-binomial")
```

This command will open the relative documentation file in the Help window of your Rstudio session.

## Format of the Dataset

Dataset can be provided as a numerical data.frame where individual information are organised by row.
Individuals with tagged with the same `"house_id"` in the respective column are considered to belong to same household.
Additionally, an individual identifier `"id"` can be provided within the respective column.

To perform model inference, a `"status"` must be provided for each individual $i$.
Status $s_{i}$ should be an integer value satisfying the following convention:

| Status $s_{i}$ | Compartment | Serology     |
|:--------------:|-------------|--------------|
| `>0`           | infectious  | seropositive |
| `0`            | susceptible | seronegative |
| `<0` or `NA`   | missing     | missing      |

### Import a Dataset

The most direct way to associate a dataset to a model is assigning it to the active method `$dataset`.
The `housepi` package comes with a few synthetic datasets to be used for testing.

```{r}
# import dataset from R6 active field
hhmodel$dataset <- housepi::survey
```
Alternatively, we can pipe such call by using wrapper `add_dataset()`. 
We can extract summary information about the current dataset with `summarise()`:

```{r}
# show a summary of the dataset as a `flextable`
hhmodel |>
  summarise() |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::theme_vanilla() |>
  flextable::set_formatter(pct = function(x) round(x, 1)) |>
  flextable::merge_v(j = ~ type) |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ type + comment, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::labelizor(labels = c(type = "", comment = "", pct = "[%]")) |>
  flextable::bg(bg = "white", part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

To learn more about `flextable` objects and how to export or format them, see [flextable](https://cloud.r-project.org/web/packages/flextable/).

At any moment we can export the dataset from our model calling `$dataset`.

## Parameter Definitions

Here we show how to provide a single parameter definition (prior and proposer rule needed for the Bayesian Monte Carlo).
Different approached are available to perform the same operation, we can define the method `$add_parameter()` in place, or pipe with the homonyme function.

```{r}
# alpha : community transmission rate
hhmodel <- hhmodel |> 
  add_parameter(name = "alpha", # name matching the model source
                prior = "unif", # uniform prior
                rule = "lnorm") # mcmc proposer rule

# beta : in-household person to person transmission rate
hhmodel$add_parameter(name = "beta", prior = "unif", rule = "lnorm")
```

At any moment we can turn a parameter definition into a constant definition: it is sufficient to set the argument `const = TRUE` (in such case a `value` must be provided).

For further information on the available options for the definition of the parameter priors and MCMC proposer rule, see the vignette [Bayesian MCMC options](bayesian_mcmc_options.html).

To see how to associate group rates in heterogeneous models, see the vignette [Group Rates](group_rates.html).

For models requiring augmented variables, the definition procedure is analogous.
We broadly discuss data augmentation in [Data Augmentation](data_augmentation.html) and we present a case study in [Augment Infection Times](augment_infection_times.html).

# Inference

After having provided all necessary definitions, we can perform inference calling `infer()`.
We can then extract the posterior calling `$as_draws_df`.
This will return a [posterior](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/posterior/) `draw` object that can be used to compute estimates.

```{r}
# run the Monte Carlo specifying setup options
hhmodel <- hhmodel |>
  infer(n_steps = 20000,  # number of mcmc steps (per chain)
        n_burnin = 1000,  # steps to burn
        thin = 8,         # delay between sampling steps
        n_adapt = 1000,   # finite adaptation steps before sampling
        n_chains = 4,     # number of independent chains
        n_threads = 1,    # number of threads
        progress = FALSE) # disable progress bar

estimates <- hhmodel |> 
  # export posterior draws using an R6 field
  as_draws_df() |> 
  posterior::summarise_draws() 
estimates
```

*Note:* parallel computations are implemented with *openMP* which is not supported on latest macOS distributions, thus the option `n_threads` is not granted on such systems.

We can proceed as usual with other popolar R packages for Bayesian analysis.
For example, we can plot the draws with [bayesplot](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bayesplot/)

```{r}
# visualize the traces of the first chain with 'bayesplot'
hhmodel |> 
  as_draws_df() |> 
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace(facet_args = list(ncol = 1))
```

or to perform model comparison, we can call functions from [loo](https://cloud.r-project.org/web/packages/loo/).
We can extract the sample of pointwise loglikelihood for each household and compute for example the leave-one-out cross-validation as follows

```{r}
# LOO-CV (leave-one-out cross-validation)
hhmodel |> 
  as_house_loglike_draws_matrix() |> 
  loo::loo()
```

# Simulation

In order to produce a simulation, our models require a pre-loaded dataset for the demographic structure of the households.
We then provide parameter definitions, here we call `load_parameter_list`, particurly helpful for multiple parameter definitions.
Finally, we call `simulate()` providing a household structure from the same dataset.

```{r}
# generate a new model object to use for simulation
simulated <- new_housepi_model("chain-binomial") |>
  # define constant parameters from the inference estimates
  # note: definition without a prior assumes parameters to be constant
  load_parameter_list(
    alpha = subset(estimates, variable == "alpha")$mean,
    beta = subset(estimates, variable == "beta")$mean
  ) |>
  # build new model using the same demographic structure of dataset
  add_dataset(housepi::survey) |>
  # override status of the dataset according to simulation
  simulate()
```

## Expected Cases by Size 

We can use the simulation process to challenge the validity of the inferred model on top of the original dataset.
We do so by computing the expected numbers of cases per household size according to our posterior distribution (i. e. by producing simulations according to posterior values).

```{r}
# run simulations according to posterior traces to compute expectations
expec <- hhmodel$expec_cases_by_house_size(progress = FALSE)
```

To show both observed and expected cases by size, we can extract the formatted cases table from our output object as follows:

```{r}
# from the rest of analysis consider sizes up to 5
# to restore, call method $drop_max_house_size()
expec$set_max_house_size(5)

# return a data.frame with observed and expected cases
cases_df <- expec$formatted_cases_table

# format expected cases
combined <- cases_df$mean
mask_exp <- cases_df$mean$distr == "Expected"
mask_cols <- setdiff(names(cases_df$mean), c("house_size", "distr"))

# format mean with its lower and upper credibile interval bounds
combined[mask_exp, mask_cols] <- mapply(
  function(m, low, up) {
    ifelse(is.na(m) | is.na(low) | is.na(up), NA,
           sprintf("%.0f [%.0f, %.0f]", m, low, up))
  },
  cases_df$mean[mask_exp, mask_cols],
  cases_df$q5[mask_exp, mask_cols],
  cases_df$q95[mask_exp, mask_cols]
)

# avoid separate_header regular expression to split house_size
names(combined)[names(combined) == "house_size"] <- "size"

# generate cases by household size table
combined |>
  flextable::flextable() |>
  flextable::separate_header() |>
  flextable::theme_vanilla() |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ size, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::merge_v(j = ~ size) |>
  flextable::align(align = "center", , part = "all") |>
  flextable::labelizor(labels = c(
    size = "Size", 
    distr = "Distribution", 
    cases = "Number of cases"
  )) |>
  flextable::bg(bg = "white", part = "all") |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

We can perform a Chi-Squared test on the shown distribution as follows:

```{r}
# perform a Chi-Squared test
expec$chisq_test()
```

The $p$-value tells us that there is no significant difference between the distribution, thus we can trust our inference process.

## Secondary Attack rate

We can have a quick look at secondary attack rates of observed vs expected cases using the fields `$sar`:

```{r}
#| message: false
#| waring: false
library(ggplot2)

col_dict <- c(Expected = "coral", Observed = "black")

# extract values for secondary attack rate
expec$sar |>
  ggplot(aes(x = house_size)) +
  # expected SAR
  geom_point(aes(y = mean, color = "Expected")) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(y = mean, ymin = q5, ymax = q95, color = "Expected"), 
    width = 0.2
  ) +
  # observed SAR
  geom_point(aes(y = observed, color = "Observed")) +
  # text with observed counts
  geom_text(aes(x = house_size + 0.2, y = observed,
                label = sprintf("[%s]", counts)),
  color = col_dict["Observed"]) +
  scale_color_manual(values = col_dict) +
  labs(x = "Household Size",
       y = "Secondary Attack Rate",
       color = "")
```
